title: Conversion and caste
hookLine: the Ambedkarite movement today, and Buddhism as a path of dignity in India

cards: "Jai Bhim." In parts of India, that's how some Buddhists greet each other: victory to Bhim.
Bhim is Bhimrao Ambedkar, and his portrait hangs beside the Buddha's in some homes and community halls, and on banners at gatherings. He wears a suit and glasses and holds a book.
Why does a lawyer in a suit sit next to the Buddha? Today's story is about birth, about dignity, and about a choice a whole movement made.

teach.b: An old scene fits today. A brahmin tending his sacred fire sees the Buddha on his alms round and shouts at him to stop where he is, calling him an outcast. The Buddha doesn't defend his own family.
He asks whether the man even knows what makes an outcast. Then he answers: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. Deeds make a person either.
That is the Vasala Sutta, and the Dhammapada says much the same. As this path told some weeks ago, B. R.
Ambedkar, born into a community treated as untouchable, took refuge in the Buddha with a great crowd in Nagpur. His followers carry that choice into ordinary places.
Small viharas stand in city neighborhoods and villages, his portrait beside the Buddha's.

Study circles read his book, The Buddha and His Dhamma. Some families take the refuges and precepts together at weddings and naming ceremonies. Each year, on the anniversary, crowds return to the ground in Nagpur.
At gatherings you'll hear his call: educate, agitate, organize.
For many in the movement, dignity means schooling, work and fair treatment as well as the refuges, and some describe Buddhism as the path that gave it all a name.
People of other traditions in India, Hindus among them, have also worked against caste; this isn't a contest between faiths.
It's the story of people told by birth that they were less, who now greet each other with two words: Jai Bhim.
So a hard week ends: Tibet in exile, Cambodia rebuilt, Saigon told with care, Mongolia and China reopening, Bamiyan's empty niches, and a path chosen for dignity. Every day, something kept.

how: Ambedkarite Buddhists gather at neighborhood viharas and community halls, take the refuges and precepts together, read Ambedkar's writings in study circles, greet one another with "Jai Bhim", and some return each year to the ground in Nagpur where he took refuge.

o: the brahmin who called the Buddha an outcast
a scholar who translated the Pali canon
the leader who took refuge with a great crowd

games.q: a path of dignity: tap the pairs.
p: no one an outcast by birth

s: in the old texts, the Buddha says a person's worth comes from birth
in the Vasala Sutta he says it is deeds, not birth, that make an outcast or a brahmin.
Ambedkarite study circles read Ambedkar's own book on the Buddha
The Buddha and His Dhamma is read in groups.
the lesson says only Buddhists have opposed caste
people of other traditions, Hindus among them, have worked against caste too.

games.q: you are the Buddha on your alms round. a brahmin at his fire shouts at you to stop, calling you an outcast. what do you do?
o: ask whether he knows what makes an outcast
tell him your family is noble
games.why: he asks what an outcast is, then answers: not birth but deeds make an outcast or a brahmin.

practice: Bring to mind someone people tend to overlook, the person who cleans the building, the one who collects the trash, a neighbor others talk past, and see their face if you can.
With each in-breath, notice that they have a whole life, as full as yours; with each out-breath, wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Ambedkar. The movement he began, still alive in neighborhood viharas and study circles, where worth is measured by deeds, not by birth. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dhamma: the teaching, the second of the three refuges Ambedkar took.

carryVoice: Your line: a path of dignity. Worth is measured by deeds, not by birth. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.7 (Vasala Sutta), the brahmin Aggika Bharadvaja; not by birth but by deeds
